name: simple-enumeration
intent: Give the collection responsibility for walking itself: the client sends one enumeration message carrying the action to perform on each element, instead of computing indices, checking bounds and dereferencing elements itself.
problem: Collection walks are written as index arithmetic - for (i = 0; i < n; i++) use(xs[i]) - so every call site owns the traversal: the bounds, the step, the accessor and the termination test. Off-by-one and out-of-range defects recur, the same walk is rewritten for every collection shape, and switching representation (array, linked list, tree, cursor) breaks every client although the intent never changed. Written this way the loop also hides intent: a reader decodes counter mechanics before seeing what the loop is for.
context: Applies wherever a client must visit every element of a collection, sequence or stream: ordinary method bodies, library APIs over container-like types, and pipelines that transform, filter or reduce element sequences. It pays off most when the collection type is polymorphic or replaceable (array, set, map, tree, database cursor, lazily produced sequence) and when the same walk is repeated in many places; it is the default reading in codebases that treat hand-written index loops as a smell.
benefits: No index bookkeeping: bounds, step, termination and element access live inside the collection, so off-by-one and out-of-range defects disappear from call sites.
Intent reads directly - 'for each open order, apply the discount' instead of counter arithmetic - and the body stays at one level of abstraction.
Traversal is decoupled from representation: linked lists, trees, hash tables, generators and cursors answer the same message, so the collection can be swapped without touching clients.
The collection makes the traversal decisions it is best placed to make: iteration order, laziness, batching, caching and cursor lifetime stay inside the type instead of being re-derived per client.
Composability with the sibling enumeration messages (collect/select/reject/inject, i.e. map/filter/fold) keeps transformations as small, individually testable steps instead of one multi-purpose loop.
Works where indices do not exist at all: streams, sockets, one-shot cursors and infinite generators cannot be indexed, only enumerated.
Testability: the action is a parameter, so enumeration logic can be exercised with a recording or collecting action instead of a real collaborating object.
tradeoffs: The client loses positional control: algorithms that genuinely need the index or a neighbouring element (ring buffers, pairwise windows, parallel arrays, lookahead) must fall back to an index loop or to a pairing message.

Mutation during traversal is the classic trap and most realizations only catch it late: g_hash_table_foreach must not modify the table, Java iterators throw ConcurrentModificationException, C++ iterator invalidation is undefined behaviour, and Python lists silently skip elements. Removal usually needs a dedicated message (foreach_remove, removeIf, retainAll) or a collect-then-apply pass.

forEach-shaped messages cannot exit early: JavaScript's Array.prototype.forEach, Kotlin's forEach and the ForEach helpers ignore break and return, so a walk that must stop at the first match needs a different message (find/detect/first/any) or a plain loop.

Hidden per-element cost: a closure, delegate or functor is built and invoked per element, and deferred pipelines (LINQ, Java streams, Rust adapters, Go iterator functions) allocate iterator state and run later than the statement that declared them - awkward in hot paths and in allocation-sensitive code.
Error attribution gets harder: a stack trace or breakpoint inside a lazy pipeline or a callback points at the pipeline or the collection's traversal code, not at the loop the reader is looking for.

Over-application flattens intent: rewriting every loop as a map/filter/fold chain produces dense expressions that are harder to read, debug and profile than the loop they replaced, especially when the chain is built only to be enumerated once for its side effects.

participants.responsibility: Owns the elements and the traversal order; answers the enumeration message and decides how the walk happens (direct, lazy, indexed, batched or remote).
One successive value handed to the action; a plain element, an entry (key/value pair) or a value derived during the walk.
The caller-supplied operation applied to each element; in languages without closures it is a function pointer plus a context object carrying the caller's state.

Optional cursor the collection creates when the protocol is cursor-based (__next__, Iterator<T>, IEnumerator<T>, next()): yields elements one at a time, signals exhaustion and owns the traversal state.
Sends the single message with the action instead of owning index state; sees only elements, never the representation.
Present for the transforming messages (collect/select/inject, map/filter/fold): accumulates or updates the derived value the message returns.

use_cases: Walking a domain collection inside a method - summing order lines, applying a rule to each entry - instead of writing a counter loop.
Exposing an aggregate as enumerable while keeping its backing store hidden: the aggregate answers each/forEach, clients never see the internal list.
Streaming and lazily produced sequences - files, sockets, database cursors, generators, Go 1.23 iterator functions - where no index exists and the producer must be driven by the consumer.
Cross-language collection APIs that must serve arrays, sets, maps and trees with one idiom (each / forEach / for-in / for...of) rather than a loop per type.
Batch transformations built from the sibling messages: map/filter/reduce chains keep each step small, named and individually testable.
Framework or library code that must apply a caller-supplied action to a collection it owns: callbacks, listeners, visitors-lite and event fan-out, where the collection hands each element over.

Ruby makes the pattern a language contract: a class that includes Enumerable and implements each receives collect/map, select, reject, inject/reduce, zip and lazy enumeration for free, so the class author writes exactly one traversal - the collection's own each (ruby-doc.org).

Go 1.23 range-over-func sells enumeration as a library product: packages hand out iter.Seq/iter.Seq2 functions and callers write 'for v := range seq()'; early exit is the yield contract itself (the yield function returns false), and the standard library (slices, maps, containers, sync) ships its traversals in this shape.

Java encodes the message at the root of its type system: every Iterable gains forEach(Consumer) as a default method whose specified behaviour is literally for (T t : this) action.accept(t), so any type that supplies iterator() answers the enumeration message without implementing it (Java SE 8, java.lang.Iterable).
avoid_when: The walk needs the index, a position or a neighbour element - a plain index loop (or a windowed/zip message) says exactly what it does and is cheaper.
The iteration must stop early and the language's forEach-shaped message cannot break - use a for/for-in statement, find/first, or a short-circuiting message instead.
Elements must be mutated in place in an index-addressable collection - a direct index loop expresses the mutation more precisely than a callback with captured state.
Only one fixed element is wanted (first, last, by key): enumerating everything to serve a lookup is the wrong message; use the dedicated accessor.
The walk is a numeric kernel over an array that the compiler must vectorise - callback-based enumeration usually blocks the optimisation; keep the raw loop.

The action needs to suspend, await or resume between elements in a language whose enumeration protocol is synchronous (a plain forEach cannot be awaited per element; use the language's async iteration form).
anti_patterns: Reinventing the walk: hand-written cursor or index loops over collections that already answer an enumeration message, re-introducing exactly the traversal defects the pattern removes.
Building a lazy pipeline only to call forEach on it: the deferred machinery, iterator allocations and harder stack traces are paid for a walk a plain loop would do.

Mutating the collection from inside the action ('add to the list while iterating'), which is undefined behaviour, a ConcurrentModificationException or a silently skipped element depending on the language.
Loop-idiom drift: the same walk written five ways in one codebase (index loop, for-each, forEach with callback, map().forEach(), manual iterator), so no reader recognises the intended idiom.
Faking early exit inside a callback-only message with a boolean flag and if-guards, hiding the real control flow that a detect/find message or a plain loop would show.
Wrapping a bare array in an enumeration object with no behaviour of its own - ceremony that adds a type without hiding anything.
design_principles: Information hiding: clients see elements, never the representation, its bounds or its cursor.
Single responsibility: traversal belongs to the collection, the per-element operation belongs to the client.
Substitutability (Liskov): any collection answering the same enumeration message is interchangeable for the caller.
Don't repeat yourself: one traversal implementation per collection instead of one per call site.
Separation of concerns (higher-order functions): the walk is decoupled from the operation performed on each element.
best_practices: Name the message after the collection and what it does (linesDo:, each, forEach) so the call site reads as intent rather than mechanism.
Use the transforming messages when a result is wanted (collect/map, select/where, inject/fold) instead of accumulating into a temporary inside do:/forEach.
Prefer the language's for-each statement when the walk needs break, continue or return; reserve forEach-shaped messages for terminal, side-effecting steps.
Never modify the collection from inside the action; collect the changes and apply them after the walk, or use the dedicated removal message (removeIf, foreach_remove, retainAll).
Keep the action small and named after its intent, and name the block parameter 'each' (or after the domain role) so nested walks remain readable.

Choose the protocol deliberately and stay consistent within a module: for-each statements for imperative bodies, streams/LINQ/iterator adapters for declarative pipelines, index loops only where the position is part of the algorithm.
Expose enumeration on aggregates instead of their backing collections, so callers cannot reorder, resize or clear the internal store.
